Feeding windows and exposed beds follow the ebb; moon phase grades the springs and neaps your week will see.
The lunar day is ~24 h 50 min (the Moon orbits while Earth spins), so semidiurnal tides beat every ~12 h 25 min and drift ~50 min later daily — arithmetic you can verify against any week's table.

At new and full moon, Sun and Moon pull together: higher highs, lower lows (springs). At the quarter moons they pull at right angles: gentler neaps. The phase calendar predicts the fortnight's character, not its centimetres.

faq: No — heights and exact local times come from official tide tables for your port, which this page points you toward rather than imitating. Context here, authority there.
Why do tides follow the Moon, not the Sun?
The Moon is far closer, so its tidal pull wins despite its size. The Sun modulates — hence springs at alignment (new/full) and neaps at quarters.
What are spring tides? (Not the season.)
The fortnightly big tides near new and full moon — 'spring' from the old word for leap/rise, unrelated to March.
No — semidiurnal (two a day) dominates the Atlantic; the Gulf of Mexico leans diurnal (one a day); parts of the Pacific mix both. Your coast's type is in its official table.
How late does high tide get each day?
About 50 minutes later per day on semidiurnal coasts, tracking the Moon's ~24 h 50 min day.
Sun times at the coast — why included?
Dawn patrols, golden-hour beach photos and safe returns all hang on the same day's light. One page, whole shore day.
Can I plan a tidal-island visit from this?
Use this for the rhythm, then confirm the exact safe window in the official table for that island — causeway crossings are not a place for estimates.
